newsitem.title: USA: Mob turncoat Gravano to testify in NY trial.
newsitem.headline: Mob turncoat Gravano to testify in NY trial.

text.p: Mob turncoat Salvatore "Sammy the Bull" Gravano will testify in the trial of a reputed New York mobster without facing questions about money he may have made from publication of his memoirs, a judge ruled on Monday.

U.S. District Judge Jack Weinstein said he does not want any "loose ends" in the federal murder and racketeering trial of Vincent "The Chin" Gigante and said he would call Gravano as a court witness if neither the defence nor prosecutors summoned him to testify.

Gravano allegedly can testify that as former underboss of the Gambino crime family he met with Gigante, who was allegedly running the Genovese crime family. Gravano reportedly was reluctant to testify because he was concerned about possible questions regarding whether he was paid for "Underboss," written in collaboration with author Peter Maas.
"(You) can't go into where he has his money stashed but everything else (you) can inquire about," the judge told lawyers for both sides at a hearing in Brooklyn federal court.
Under New York's "Son of Sam" laws, which limit the ability of convicted criminals to profit from accounts of their crimes, Gravano could not keep any money he was paid.

He confessed to 19 murders as part of his deal with the government to testify against reputed mobsters for at least two years. He spent five years in prison and has now left the federal witness protection programme but remains in hiding.
Testimony from Gravano was critical in the 1992 murder and racketeering conviction of reputed Gambino godfather John Gotti, who is serving life in prison without parole.
Gigante, who faces a 21-count murder and racketeering indictment, is one of the last old-time reputed mob dons with a strong sense of tradition.

He is accused of ordering the killing of seven people and conspiring to kill three others, allegedly to avenge breaches of protocol such as unauthorised slayings. Known more recently for wandering around New York's Greenwich Vilage neighbourhood muttering to himself and wearing a dirty, tattered bathrobe, Gigante, 69, has earned himself the nichname "The Oddfather."
His attorneys say he has been incapacitated by mental illness for years, but prosecutors say he has feigned illness to avoid prosecution and is in fact lucid and shrewd.

The judge said two other mob turncoats would testify in the Gigante trial. One is Anthony "Gaspipe" Casso, a former Lucchese family underboss who has admitted to 39 murders. He is expected to testify that he met with Gigante as a member of the New York mob hierarchy.

The other is Vincent "Fish" Cafaro, a former Genovese soldier who allegedly can identify Gigante as the family boss. So far in the two-week trial, two informants have failed to link Gigante directly with the charges in the indictment.
One was Peter "Big Pete" Chiodo, a former Lucchese capo who began cooperating after surviving a murder attempt. He testified about a scheme to rig bidding on city contracts.

The other was Philip "Crazy Phil" Leonetti, a former Philadelphia family underboss now in witness protection. He testified that Gigante ordered several Philadelphia murders but admitted he never met directly with him.
The trial is expected to continue for another three weeks. If convicted, Gigante faces the possibility of life in prison.
